hypothesis: Wisconsin's brandy culture crosses the Mississippi: brandy share rises the closer an Iowa county is to Wisconsin.
test: OLS of brandy share on -log(1+miles to WI border) + 4 controls, HC3 + Freedman-Lane permutation, 2025 & 2026
effect: WI-border counties 2.7% brandy vs 1.6% elsewhere (1.7x); Spearman(distance, share) = -0.31

hypothesis: Taste is contagious: after removing demographics, neighbouring counties still drink alike (spatially clustered residuals).
test: Moran's I of OLS residuals (family share ~ 4 controls + %Hispanic + MO border), queen adjacency, 2,000 permutations, each year
effect: 2/8 families clustered in both years: whiskey I=0.142, rum I=0.167

hypothesis: Border leakage has a travel-cost horizon: liters per adult rise with distance from Missouri, then flatten beyond a measurable break.
test: Hinge regression log(L/adult) ~ min(miles to MO, k) + controls; k grid-searched 10-200 mi; bootstrap (500) for k
effect: break ~30 mi in 2026 (90% CI [30, 195]), 195 mi in 2025; +33.9% liters/adult per 10 mi inside the break

hypothesis: Religion leaves a fingerprint: Dutch-Reformed Sioux County buys far less than its demographics, store count and border position predict.
test: Externally studentised residual of Sioux County in log(L/adult) ~ controls + MO border + log(stores/10k adults), both years
effect: Sioux buys -7% vs prediction (2026), rank 40/99 (2025 rank 44); studentised resid -0.23

hypothesis: St Patrick's Day is visible in wholesale data: Irish whiskey's share jumps in Feb-Mar orders, while Scotch (same shelf, no holiday) does not.
test: Store-level paired Wilcoxon: Irish share Feb-Mar vs Apr-Oct, each year; Scotch as placebo
effect: Irish share +29% (2026), +24% (2025) vs Scotch +4%; peak month share 1.84% (2026-02) vs median 1.16%

hypothesis: The Cinco de Mayo agave bump is bigger in counties with more Hispanic residents.
test: County log-uplift of agave share (Apr 14-May 4 vs flanking 3-week windows) regressed on %Hispanic + controls, each year
effect: statewide agave-share bump +16.2% (2026), +7.9% (2025); Hispanic slope +0.181 log-pts per +10 pts
verdict: REJECTED - bump exists but is no larger in Hispanic counties

hypothesis: College towns empty out: Ames and Iowa City order far less in Jun-Jul relative to Sep-Oct than any normal county (students leave, football returns).
test: County ratio log[(Jun+Jul)/(Sep+Oct) liters]; rank of Story & Johnson among 99; P(both ranks this low by chance)
effect: 2026: Story -37%, Johnson -25% vs median county; ranks 2 & 4/99

hypothesis: The holiday gift economy is a rich-county thing: the Nov-Dec jump in premium share grows with county income.
test: County change in premium share (Nov-Dec 2025 minus Jan-Oct 2025, pp) ~ income + controls, HC3 + permutation (one holiday season available)
effect: statewide premium share 24.8% -> 27.1%; +-0.00 pp per +$10k income; holiday mix: brandy +14%, liqueur +9%, rtd -33%

hypothesis: Iowa rotates its palate with the seasons: RTD, rum, agave, gin and vodka gain share in summer; whiskey, liqueur and brandy in winter.
test: Store-level paired Wilcoxon of family shares, summer (Jun-Aug 25/26) vs winter (Nov 25-Jan 26), direction pre-stated per family
effect: rtd +48%, rum -3%, agave +9%, vodka +6%, liqueur -6%, brandy -7%, whiskey -6%, gin +14%

hypothesis: State price cuts mostly move orders in time: retailers stock up during a temporary cost cut and then under-order once it ends.
test: Item x month two-way fixed effects, 2,251 regularly stocked items, clean-price months only (Jul-Oct 25, Feb-Oct 26), SEs clustered by item; promo = cost >=5% below item's modal cost
effect: orders +14% in promo months (median cut 12%, implied arc elasticity -1.0); +49% the month after; +1% the month before
verdict: REJECTED - timing is reversed: the surge comes the month AFTER the cut (p=7.3e-08), no hangover

hypothesis: The 2025-26 tariff era shows up on the shelf: same-item wholesale costs rose more for imported spirits than for American ones.
test: Same-item modal state cost Jul-Oct 2026 vs Jul-Oct 2025 by origin (from category); Mann-Whitney imports vs USA (cost is blank Jan-Jun 2025)

hypothesis: Inequality builds a barbell: high-Gini counties buy a wider spread of price tiers (more bottom shelf AND more top shelf), not a higher average.
test: County liter-weighted SD of log price/L ~ Gini + controls (and mean log price as the contrast), both years
effect: SD: +0.0038 per Gini point (2026), +0.0036 (2025); mean price: +0.0081 (SUPPORTED (both years); not under pop. weights)
verdict: PARTIAL - spread widens, but the average price rises too (both years); not under pop. weights

hypothesis: The 50 ml 'nip' is a poverty index: poorer counties spend a larger share on mini bottles, even comparing stores of the same type.
test: County dollar share of <=50 ml bottles ~ poverty rate + controls + convenience-store share (both years); store-level with store-type FE, clustered by county
effect: +-0.13% mini share per +10 pts poverty (county, 2026); store-level within type +3.30% (p=0.019)
verdict: PARTIAL - holds within store type (store level), not across counties

hypothesis: More outlets, more drinking - but only partly: liters per adult rise with store density with an elasticity well below 1, matching H3's finding that ~60% of a new store's volume is stolen.
test: County log(L/adult) ~ log(stores per 10k adults) + controls + MO border, both years; compare elasticity to 1 - 0.60 = 0.40 implied by H3

hypothesis: The long tail lives in cities: for the same number of order lines, dense counties buy many more distinct products and are less dominated by a few suppliers.
test: Rarefaction: distinct SKUs in 892 random 2026 order lines per county (20 draws) ~ log density + controls; vendor HHI as second outcome
effect: +75 distinct SKUs per log-unit of density; densest decile 547 vs sparsest 322 SKUs; vendor HHI slope +0.0019

hypothesis: Spirits obey Zipf's law: product volume falls as 1/rank, so a tiny head of SKUs carries the state and the head is stable year to year.
test: OLS log(liters) ~ log(rank), ranks 10-1000, 2026; Pareto shares; Spearman of top-100 volumes 2025 vs 2026
effect: slope -1.10 (95% CI -1.11 to -1.09; Zipf = -1); top 1% of 4,792 SKUs = 38% of liters, top 20% = 91%; top-100 stability rho = 0.93

hypothesis: New stores have a honeymoon: the opening order (empty shelves being filled) overshoots the store's steady-state monthly level, so a forecast built on it overshoots.
test: Liters in months 0-6 after first order / mean of months 3-5, for genuinely new stores (first order Mar 2025-Apr 2026); one-sided Wilcoxon
effect: median ratio by month since opening: m0=1.86, m1=0.79, m2=0.89, m3=0.94, m4=0.95, m5=0.98, m6=0.98 (n=191)
verdict: SUPPORTED - and followed by a dip below steady state in month 1

hypothesis: Stores die slowly, not suddenly: in the 3 months before their last order, exiting stores' volume and product range shrink well below their own seasonal norm - an early-warning signal.
test: 142 stores whose last order was <= Jul 2026: season-adjusted volume (last 3 full months vs previous 6), SKU count ratio; AUC of the decline as a 3-month exit predictor
effect: median volume -6%, median SKU range -5% before exit; early-warning AUC = 0.53
verdict: MOSTLY REJECTED - the decline is small and useless as a warning: stores die suddenly

hypothesis: Customers belong to the address, not the owner: when a shop changes hands, the new licensee's product mix is far closer to its predecessor's than to any random store of the same type.
test: Jensen-Shannon distance of family mix: 55 predecessor->successor pairs at the same address vs random same-type pairs; Mann-Whitney
effect: median JS distance 0.123 at same address vs 0.254 random same-type (49% of it); successor's monthly volume = 92% of predecessor's

hypothesis: Iowa's whiskey divide is generational: within the whiskey aisle, Canadian whisky's share rises with a county's median age and bourbon's share falls, after controlling for density, income and education.
test: County share of whiskey liters (Canadian; bourbon) ~ median age + log density + income + % bachelor's, HC3 + permutation, both years
effect: Canadian is Iowa's #2 category overall; oldest-quintile counties 60% Canadian / 19% bourbon vs youngest 51% / 23%; with controls, +5 yrs median age: Canadian -2.3% pts, bourbon +0.4% pts (2026); instead 10x density = -21% pts Canadian (r=-0.69), +10 pts bachelor's = +4% pts bourbon
verdict: REJECTED - age is only a proxy: rurality drives Canadian, education drives bourbon
